opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes down to where the bottleneck actually is. Everyone talks about models and data, but when you look at how a research idea becomes something that runs at scale, a huge amount of time goes into the layer underneath: getting a new attention variant, a new optimizer, or some unusual sparsity pattern to run efficiently on the hardware. Right now that depends on a small number of people who deeply understand both the math and the memory hierarchy of the chip. That doesn't scale, and it quietly shapes which ideas get tried at all. If something is awkward to write a fast kernel for, people often don't explore it.

So the motivation is partly about speed and partly about widening the space of ideas. If you can describe the computation at a high level and get a kernel that's correct and close to hand-tuned performance, the loop from "I have an idea" to "I have a real result at scale" gets much shorter. You stop making architecture decisions based on what's convenient to implement.

It's also a good problem for current models. Kernel generation has a tight feedback signal: you can check correctness against a reference implementation, and you can measure performance directly. That's a lot more tractable than many open-ended tasks, because you can search, verify, and iterate automatically instead of relying on fuzzy judgment.

And there's compounding value. Better kernels make training and inference cheaper, which frees up compute for the next round of research, including better models for writing kernels. That kind of flywheel is exactly what you want to prioritize over a six-month horizon, because the payoff doesn't stay in one project. It spreads across everything the team does.

r001.rationale: The response says implementation difficulty can prevent ideas from being explored, but it does not clearly state that an architecture’s quality alone fails to ensure adoption.

r002.rationale: It says high-level computations could become efficient kernels, shortening the loop from an idea to a result at scale.

r003.rationale: It identifies reliance on a small number of people with deep math and hardware expertise as a bottleneck that does not scale.

r004.rationale: It does not say current AI coding models cannot match expert-led QR kernel optimization; it instead describes kernel generation as tractable for current models and targets close-to-hand-tuned performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the simplest answer is that kernels are where a huge amount of our compute efficiency actually gets decided, and right now that work is bottlenecked on a very small number of people.

Think about what it takes to train or serve a frontier model today. You have a new attention variant, a new MoE routing scheme, some fused normalization, a quantization format that didn't exist six months ago. Every one of those needs a kernel that's tuned to the specific hardware generation, the specific memory hierarchy, the specific shapes you actually run. And the people who can write a really good one, who understand tensor core scheduling, shared memory banking, register pressure, the whole stack, you can count them on a couple of hands at most companies. So what happens in practice is that the research velocity gets throttled by kernel velocity. A researcher has an idea, and the honest answer is "that's a two-week kernel project, get in line."

The second reason is that it's one of the places where I think models are genuinely good enough now to help. Kernel writing has properties that make it almost ideal for automated generation. You have a hard correctness check, because you can compare against a reference implementation on random inputs. You have a scalar objective, which is wall-clock time or throughput. And you have a search space that's large but structured. That's exactly the setup where you can let a model propose, run it, measure, and iterate. You don't need a human in the loop to tell you whether the output is good. The hardware tells you.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that the target keeps moving. Every new accelerator generation changes the trade-offs. Code that was optimal eighteen months ago is often leaving twenty, thirty percent on the table today. If you depend on humans to re-tune everything by hand each cycle, you're perpetually behind. If you have a system that can regenerate and re-tune as the hardware changes, that cost becomes much closer to an afternoon of compute than a quarter of engineering time.

So when I think about what moves the needle for Core AI over six months, I'm looking for leverage. Something where a focused investment compounds across every team that touches a GPU. Kernel generation is that. It makes the researchers faster, it makes the infra cheaper, and it's a problem shape where we can actually measure whether we're winning. That combination is pretty rare, and that's why it's near the top of the list.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that architecture quality alone fails to ensure adoption.

r002.rationale: It says research ideas are delayed by kernel work and that generation makes researchers faster, describing a shorter path from an idea to a tuned GPU kernel.

r003.rationale: It identifies high-performance kernel expertise as scarce, saying qualified people can be counted on a few hands and that research velocity is throttled by kernel velocity.

r004.rationale: The response says models are capable of proposing, testing, measuring, and iterating on kernels, and does not state that they cannot independently match expert-led QR optimization.

astra-6.text:
Because the gap between a model idea and an efficient implementation is still too large. You can come up with a promising architecture, but if it requires a new kernel, you’re suddenly dependent on scarce expertise and a lot of manual tuning. That slows down both experimentation and deployment.

Automated kernel generation has the potential to shorten that loop. You describe the computation, generate candidate implementations, check correctness, and measure performance on the hardware you actually care about. The measurement is essential—you want something that’s demonstrably faster, not just code that looks plausible.

For a six-month roadmap, I’d focus on making that loop reliable for a bounded set of important workloads. If we can reduce the engineering effort required to get good performance, we free researchers to try more ideas and make the compute we already have more useful. That’s why I see it as a priority.

r001.rationale: It says a promising architecture may require a new kernel and that manual tuning and scarce expertise slow experimentation and deployment, conveying that architecture quality alone does not ensure adoption.

r002.rationale: It says automated kernel generation can shorten the loop from describing a computation to generating, checking, and measuring efficient implementations.

r003.rationale: It identifies dependence on scarce expertise and manual tuning as obstacles to obtaining good performance.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss current AI coding models or compare their optimization ability with expert-led QR kernel work.

sol-6.1.text:
Because kernels are where a lot of the gap between what hardware promises and what our models actually achieve shows up. You can have a good model architecture, but if its operations don’t map efficiently onto the GPU, you leave performance on the table. Closing that gap manually takes specialized engineering, and you have to revisit the work as models and hardware change.

Automated kernel generation could make that iteration much faster. The goal is to generate a candidate, check that it’s correct, measure it on the actual hardware, and improve it based on those results. Generating code is only one part of that loop; verification and measurement are essential.

For a six-month roadmap, I’d focus on demonstrating reliable gains on a bounded set of important workloads. If we can do that, we can reduce the cost of experimentation and give researchers more room to try ideas without every new operation becoming a substantial optimization project.

r001.rationale: The response says inefficient GPU mapping leaves performance on the table, but does not state that architecture quality alone fails to ensure adoption.

r002.rationale: It connects architecture ideas to efficient GPU mapping and says automated generation can speed the iteration of generating, checking, measuring, and improving kernels.

r003.rationale: It mentions that manual optimization takes specialized engineering, but does not identify exceptionally scarce human expertise as a bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss AI coding models, QR kernels, or a comparison with expert-led optimization.
